Chapter 2: Expanding Options Beyond the Obvious
So, once you've learned to spot those common decision-making traps, what's next? It's all about deliberately widening your field of options before you commit to a choice. You know, the real problem with so many decisions isn't that we pick the wrong thing—it's that the best choice never even makes it onto our radar.
Imagine standing at a fork in the road, convinced there are only two directions you can go. But what if, just out of sight, there are hidden trails, side roads, or even the chance to build a brand-new path? The trick is to look past the obvious and ask yourself, "What else could I do?"
One simple but powerful technique is to ask, "What would I do if this option wasn't on the table?" That question shakes things up. Suddenly, your mind has to get creative and look for alternatives you might've missed. Like, think about a student choosing between two universities. If neither school accepted them, what then? Maybe they'd consider a gap year, look at different programs, or try out an internship instead.
Here's another strategy—try looking for “and” instead of just “or.” Instead of feeling stuck between two competing ideas, see if you can do a bit of both. Picture a business leader torn between investing in product development or marketing. What if they could run a small pilot project while launching a marketing campaign at the same time? Sometimes, blending options leads to the most innovative results.
You can also borrow ideas from other fields. If a nonprofit is struggling to recruit volunteers, why not check out how sports teams or local clubs attract new members? Sometimes, the best solutions come from places you'd never expect. Looking outside your usual circles can help you break out of those familiar ruts.
And don't forget the power of getting other people involved. When you bring in folks with different backgrounds or fresh perspectives, they’ll often see possibilities you might have missed. If your team is stuck, invite an outsider to look over your options, or just ask your colleagues, "What are we not seeing?" That one simple question can open up a whole world of creative alternatives.
Here are a few practical ways to expand your options:
First, consider the opposite. Challenge your current assumptions and look for reasons why your go-to options might not be the best. Seek out alternatives that shake up the status quo.
Second, explore opportunity cost. Ask yourself what you're giving up by choosing one path over another—and whether those sacrifices really make sense.
And finally, run small experiments. Instead of going all-in on one approach, test out several on a smaller scale to see which works best for you.
So, what's the bottom line here? By making it a habit to broaden your choices, you can dodge the trap of false dilemmas—and give yourself a real shot at finding the solution that fits just right. Remember, it's not about making things more complicated. It's about giving yourself the chance to discover options you might have never considered.
